entities.name: Celsus
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Celsus, a Roman usurper, briefly seized imperial power in Africa during the tumultuous reign of Emperor Gallienus in 265 CE, a period marked by civil strife and external threats known as the Crisis of the Third Century. His ephemeral seven-day rule, though swiftly crushed, underscores the profound instability plaguing the Roman Empire, where provincial governors and military commanders frequently challenged central authority, contributing to the fragmentation of imperial control. His story, primarily preserved through the *Historia Augusta*, illustrates the precarious nature of imperial power and the constant threat of rebellion from within the vast Roman territories.

According to the *Historia Augusta*, Celsus was a former military tribune and tribune of the plebs, described as a man of considerable stature and moral uprightness. His elevation to emperor was not self-proclaimed but initiated by Vivius Macrianus, procurator of Mauretania, and other local officials in Africa, who sought to replace the distant and often perceived as ineffective Emperor Gallienus. Proclaimed emperor in the Roman province of Africa, Celsus's brief reign was a desperate attempt by local elites to assert autonomy or secure stability amidst the empire's disarray, a common pattern during the mid-3rd century.

The swift suppression of Celsus's usurpation, reportedly orchestrated by the loyalists of Galliena (a relative of the emperor, possibly Gallienus's wife Salonina, acting as governor), culminated in his death within a week of his acclamation. His head was subsequently paraded through the streets of Carthage, serving as a stark warning against further insurrections. While Celsus himself left no lasting political or military legacy, his short-lived rebellion contributed to the broader narrative of the Crisis of the Third Century, highlighting the systemic weaknesses and the decentralization of power that threatened to dismantle the Roman state.
